Tested conduct and sound teaching must answer disruption within households

Verses 6–8 describe an elder’s home and character. Verse 9 adds what he must do with the teaching. He must hold to the faithful word as he was taught. That gives him two abilities. He can encourage with sound doctrine, and he can refute those who contradict. Verses 10–11 show why both are needed in Crete. Teachers there upset whole households, and their mouths must be stopped.
Grace supplies the reason for instruction and eagerness to do good

Verses 2–10 give instructions to five groups in the household. Verse 11 begins with “for” and gives the ground: God’s grace has appeared. Verse 12 says grace trains people to deny ungodliness and live soberly. Verse 14 names the act behind that grace. Christ “gave himself for us.” Two purposes follow: to redeem from all iniquity and to purify a people. That people is marked by one trait: zeal for good works.
Received mercy directs attention from disputes toward work that meets needs

Verses 4–7 say God saved by mercy and not by works done in righteousness. Verse 8 calls this a faithful saying and tells Titus to insist on it. The purpose is that believers be careful to do good works. Works do not earn the mercy; they follow it. The verse calls them good and profitable to people. Verse 9 names the contrast: disputes about the law are unprofitable. Verse 14 gives the practical form: good works that meet pressing needs.
